<reason>Side B won decisively by dismantling Side A's unit-economics math and trapping Side A in a fatal dilemma over buyer-side return fraud. Side B showed that platforms already authenticate high-ticket luxury items (neutralizing Side A's $2,000 Chanel example as status quo), and proved that pushing physical authentication down into everyday resale fails because percentage commissions shrink while two-way shipping and human inspection remain flat physical costs. When Side A tried to avoid universal warehouse costs by proposing "photo forensics" and "tiered fees," Side B exposed how photo forensics contradicted Side A's own opening claim about photos being inadequate, could not prove whether a seller shipped a fake or a buyer swapped the item post-delivery, and admitted that consumers would ultimately bear higher fees.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B4.3]-[B4.5], Side B dismantled Side A's Rebuttal 2 answers by showing that "tiering fees" concedes consumer fee hikes, casual closet sellers cannot "batch shipments," and relying on "photo forensics" both contradicts Side A's opening premise [A1.1] and fails to tell whether a dishonest buyer swapped an uninspected garment before photographing it.</best_rebuttal>
